findings.title: Routine cleanup info logged at Error level
findings.body: The new code in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags uses r.log.Error for messages that describe normal operation, e.g. 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags'. These fire on every successful cleanup batch and are not errors. Using Error level will pollute error monitoring/dashboards (anything watching for Error-level entries will be noisy/alarmed) and may cause on-call pages. The 'err' key is also always passed in, even when err is nil. These should be r.log.Info or r.log.Debug. Logging every ID at error level also risks leaking IDs into permanent error stores.

findings.title: annotationType interpolated into SQL without validation
findings.body: In CleanAnnotations, the annotationType argument is interpolated directly into the WHERE clause via fmt.Sprintf: cond := fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, ...). annotationType is an interface-typed string parameter with no allow-list or validation in fetchIDs; any caller passing untrusted input gets a SQL injection. This pattern was inherited from the old code but is now reused via fetchIDs which itself does fmt.Sprintf(` WHERE %s`, condition). At minimum the helpers should reject table/condition values that don't match an expected allow-list or constant set (e.g. alertAnnotationType, dashboardAnnotationType, apiAnnotationType), or the SQL should be composed with bound parameters instead of string formatting.

findings.title: O(n^2) string building in SQLite inline-id path
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size > 999, the code builds the IN-list by repeatedly calling fmt.Sprintf('%s, %d', values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration allocates a new string of length O(i), giving O(n^2) work and O(n^2) intermediate allocations. For a batch of 32767 IDs this is on the order of a billion character copies. Use strings.Builder or a single fmt.Sprintf with a precomputed separator, or strings.Join over strconv formatted values. The new integration test exercises exactly this path with 32767 IDs, so the cost will show up in CI and any production SQLite deployment configured with a large batch size.

findings.title: deleteByIDs chooses inlined SQL by configured batch size, not actual id count
findings.body: deleteByIDs switches to the inlined-SQL branch when r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit. The branch should depend on len(ids), not on the configured batch size: if the operator has set a large batch size but a particular batch returns only a handful of ids (common when there are few rows left to clean), we still go down the inlined-SQL path and pay the O(n^2) cost for no benefit. Conversely, if the operator mis-configures AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize to be small (<= 999) while the actual returned ids somehow exceed that (e.g. via a future change), we would silently use the parameterized path and potentially exceed SQLite's parameter limit. Use len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit as the gate.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to deadlock fix
findings.body: The ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1 with no comment and no relation to the MySQL deadlock being addressed. This is a 10x increase in how often the cleanup job runs, and combined with this PR's split-into-two-statements change each cleanup now performs roughly 2x more DB round trips per batch. On large annotation tables this can substantially increase database load, lock contention, and log volume. The 9-minute cleanup context timeout also means a single slow run (made slower by the new strategy) is much more likely to be cancelled. This belongs in its own PR with justification, or at least a comment explaining the rationale, and ideally should be configurable rather than a hard-coded 1-minute default.

findings.title: SELECT-then-DELETE allows under-deletion with concurrent writes
findings.body: After fetching the ids, the delete runs in a separate statement and separate session. A concurrent transaction can insert new annotations that satisfy the same cleanup predicate (MaxAge cutoff or MaxCount offset) between fetch and delete; those new rows will not be in the fetched id set and so will not be deleted this cycle. The author documented this as 'may under-delete... any such annotations will simply be cleaned on the next cycle', which is acceptable, but the test suite does not exercise this scenario (no concurrent inserter) and there is no log/instrumentation that would let an operator detect persistent under-deletion. Worth noting so it isn't quietly relied on as exact enforcement.

findings.title: t.Cleanup uses assert.NoError, failures don't terminate subsequent subtests
findings.body: The new per-subtest t.Cleanup deletes annotation and annotation_tag rows via session.Exec and then calls assert.NoError(t, err). assert.NoError only records t.Error and does not call t.FailNow, so if the DELETE silently fails (e.g., a SQL error in a future schema change), the next subtest will run against leftover data and produce confusing failures rather than failing at the cleanup site. Use require.NoError inside the cleanup so a failure surfaces immediately. Also, the subtests share the same fakeSQL but rely on sequential DELETE before the next subtest creates ids starting from 1; a missed cleanup causes primary-key conflicts on subsequent InsertMulti.

findings.title: New SQLite large-batch test is slow and may run unconditionally
findings.body: The new subtest 'should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0' creates 40003 annotations and 80006 annotation_tags, then performs a multi-batch cleanup. createTestAnnotations uses InsertMulti in batches of 500, so this requires ~80 annotation batches and ~161 tag batches, plus several cleanup cycles. This is fine on developer laptops but will add noticeable seconds to every CI run on this package. There is no t.Skip on this case and the assertion (40000 affected) depends on the exact i%3 split working out, which is fragile if the createTestAnnotations layout changes. Consider a smaller number or guarding it behind a build tag.

findings.title: Renamed tests now require a real database even for unit-style runs
findings.body: The previously-in-package TestAnnotationCleanUp and TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst were renamed to TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp and TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst and gained a t.Skip on testing.Short(). The earlier versions ran unconditionally and provided coverage of the cleanup SQL; the new versions are gated on a long mode and require the InitTestDB infra. There is no replacement test that covers the SQL composition (the cond strings, the annotationType interpolation, the MaxCount offset arithmetic) without a DB, and no test that specifically asserts the deadlock-avoidance split (id fetch + separate delete) is exercised. At minimum a table-driven unit test verifying the constructed cond strings and the Limit/LimitOffset substitution for each dialect would prevent silent regressions to the SQL the PR is trying to fix.
